data.title: Staré Město – Velehrad, Rastislav's old town of 871
data.excerpt: Staré Město near Uherské Hradiště is most probably the “old town of Rastislav” that the Annals of Fulda record for the year 871, and it also bears the older name Velehrad, first written down in 1131. By the end of the 9th century a 2 km rampart with a moat enclosed up to 250 ha here; excavation has yielded about 10,000 graves, two Moravian churches, a rotunda of St Michael and a whole range of craft workshops.
data.metaTitle: Staré Město – Velehrad, a centre of old Moravia
data.metaDescription: Staré Město near Uherské Hradiště — Rastislav's “old town” of the Annals of Fulda (871) and a great centre of production, trade and culture of old Moravia.

children.text: Staré Město has borne this name from the earliest times to the present day. In the Annals of Fulda we find a note for the year 871 that: “svatopluk went to rastislav's old town...”, when he was preparing to deceive Carloman and destroy his army. Some historians doubt that this is the actual name of the town and argue that it is a general description of some old town in Moravia. In the original Latin texts of this period the initial letters of the names of towns, countries and rivers, and of personal names too, are lower case, and so this record in itself really does not tell us with complete certainty whether it is the proper name of the town or merely a statement of the fact that Rastislav's seat was old. But some other charters in later centuries also describe this site (that is, present-day Staré Město) as the “old town”, and this name has survived to the present day.

children.text: Extensive archaeological finds from the time of old Moravia have been discovered in the area of this town, so there is no reason to doubt that the name “Staré Město” was in use in the earliest times. But one more name for this area has come down to us: “Velehrad”. Although the first written record of this name dates only from 1131, literally as “Veligrad”, it is clear that the name must be much older, going back to the period of old Moravia in the 9th century. When the Czech king Přemysl Otakar II founded present-day Uherské Hradiště in 1257, on the opposite bank of the river Morava from Staré Město, this newly founded town was given the name “New Town” or also “New Velehrad”, in order to distinguish it from the neighbouring Old Town, or the “old” Velehrad. But in the 13th century the name Velehrad also came to be used for a nearby village lying to the north-west of Uherské Hradiště, because a Cistercian monastery was founded there on Velehrad land in the 13th century. In the 13th century, then, there were already three places close to one another bearing the name “Velehrad”: Staré Město was called Velehrad, the adjoining New Town was called New Velehrad, and the nearby village that grew up around the monastery also came to be called Velehrad. Later, however, the name “Staré Město” became established and the name Velehrad fell out of use; the adjoining newly founded town with the names “New Town” or “New Velehrad” came to be called something else, “Hradiště” (and still later it came to be called Uherské Hradiště), and the names “New Town” and “New Velehrad” disappeared. The name Velehrad has nevertheless survived to this day for the nearby village with the monastery mentioned above. The original name Velehrad was therefore probably applied to this whole area, which today is the centre of the Slovácko region (see the illustration). This was probably the seat of our Moravian rulers and of high church dignitaries. Various historical documents from the 14th century onwards preserve statements that Methodius was “archbishop of Velehrad” and that Velehrad was the capital of the Moravian kingdom.

Archaeology has confirmed that this area is very ancient and that our ancestors lived here at a high cultural level. Over the last 150 years inhumation graves have been found at many places in Staré Město, containing a great deal of gold, silver and bronze jewellery, iron weapons, swords, axes, spears, knives and the typical Old Slavic pottery of fired clay. Three hoards of axe-shaped currency bars containing 23 pieces have so far been excavated in the area of Staré Město, together with more than 40 axe-shaped currency bars as individual finds. Most of these finds date from the second half of the 9th and the first half of the 10th century. But it was above all from the 1950s onwards that more intensive archaeological excavation began, which brought new information about this area. Many dwellings and production features of an agricultural and craft character were uncovered here. Approximately 10,000 graves were uncovered in several cemeteries! The foundations of two Moravian Christian churches with their cemeteries were discovered, all of them of the period of old Moravia. Around the first church about 2,000 graves with 5,000 artefacts were found, around the second 56 graves with rich finds of gold and silver jewellery. In this cemetery around the second church, then, people of the higher social strata were buried. The first church dated from before the Cyrillo-Methodian period, the second was built only after the arrival of Cyril and Methodius in old Moravia. The graves around the first church yielded 104 wheel-thrown vessels with horizontal grooves or wavy lines on the upper part of the vessel, various metal tools and weapons, bronze, silver, gilded and gold gombíky, sumptuous jewellery, and in the women's graves more than 100 gold, silver and bronze earrings of various shapes, gold and silver finger rings, and necklaces of multicoloured glass and bronze beads with gold, silver and bronze pendants.

Beneath the paving of the present Church of St Michael, which stands in the modern cemetery of Staré Město, the foundations of a 9th-century Moravian rotunda were discovered, which was certainly dedicated to the same saint. The present Church of St Michael stands partly on the foundations of this rotunda, and the collapsed building material of the original rotunda was certainly used in its construction as well. The isolated graves that could still be found here date from the 11th–12th century, which means that this site was not abandoned but has been occupied continuously to the present day.

Churches of the period of old Moravia probably stood at two further places as well. When an irrigation canal was being dug in 1936 beside the road from Staré Město to Uherské Hradiště, many dwellings were encountered here, together with some hand-worked sandstone blocks. No further attention was paid to this find, but it may have been the Church of St Clement, which historical material mentions as having stood somewhere in this area. The second church, that of St Vitus, at the locality known as “Na kostelíku”, disappeared in the 18th century and almost nothing has survived of it. Its origin may have reached back to the period of old Moravia, although this has not been confirmed so far.

children.text: The occupied area of Staré Město – Velehrad in the period of old Moravia was enormous. By the end of the 9th century the town was enclosed on its north-western side by a strong defensive rampart with a water-filled moat. In the end this defensive rampart was 2 km long and enclosed a settled area of up to 250 ha (that is, 2.5 km²). Half of the length of the defensive rampart consisted of a raised bank 7.5 m wide, into which two rows of massive tree trunks, driven tightly together, were set. The trunks were up to 40 cm thick and set 1 m into the ground. The space between the two rows of trunks was filled with earth and gravel. In addition, a moat almost 5 metres wide and 2.3 m deep was built in front of the rampart on the outer side. The whole southern side of Velehrad was protected by the river Morava and the surrounding marshy terrain (see the illustration).

Staré Město – Velehrad was a developed medieval town. Craft production in particular was at a high level. There were workshops for working antler and bone, workshops for making jewellery, and stone-working, smithing, metal-casting and pottery workshops, in which fine yellow pottery of classical form was also produced. Remains of iron-smelting and melting furnaces with forges were discovered here, as well as the foundations of a windmill for grinding grain. In many of the melting furnaces it was not raw ore that was melted but already finished metal, and it has been proved that the jewellery and the ornamental gombíky found in the graves also came from these furnaces. The finely worked gold jewellery was made in the specialised workshops of Velehrad, since drops of molten gold were found here. Many iron objects for household use were also produced, and tin was melted and cast here together with copper, giving white bronze, from which various utilitarian and ornamental objects were made.

Agriculture was also well developed, as is attested by numerous finds of grain pits and granaries and of various agricultural implements. Half of the animal bones found came from the keeping of domestic pigs; sheep, cattle, goats and poultry, especially geese, were also kept. Fishing was common. Only 8% of the animal bones came from the hunting of wild animals, so we can see that our ancestors secured both their plant and their animal food purposefully, by growing cultivated crops or by keeping domestic livestock. Further archaeological finds from Staré Město, with illustrations, are described in more detail in Vilém Hrubý's article “Antiqua civitas – Veligrad” in the book “Ochrana pamiatok 8”, published by the Slovak Institute for the Care of Monuments and the Protection of Nature in Bratislava in 1972.

It is assumed that this settlement centre existed here from the 7th century at the latest, but it was above all in the 9th century that Staré Město – Velehrad was a great centre of production, trade and culture of old Moravia.
